Correct, and for the right reason: the ambient number enters nowhere once the rate is stated intrinsically.

We're now one ingredient short of the full picture. A guarantee needs a metric — so which one?

## The default, and why it's only a default

The data arrive with coordinates, and coordinates come with an obvious ruler: Euclidean distance, $\lVert x-x'\rVert$, the norm of a difference. It's the one you'd reach for without thinking, and it is a **recording choice**, not a property of the data.

- Units. Millimetres versus metres, raw pixel values versus calibrated radiance.
- Scaling. Normalize a feature, and its axis stretches.
- Encoding. One-hot versus ordinal codes for the same category.

Same information, same points, different geometry — and the neighbour structure moves with it. This is not a subtle effect: stretch a single coordinate axis by $10\times$ and the points nearest to a query can flip completely, from the ones beside it to the ones above and below it. Nothing about the data changed. Only the ruler.

I'm having a figure built for exactly this — the same six points, twice, with the raw axes and then with one axis stretched, showing the $2$-nearest set before and after. It'll land shortly and you can see the flip rather than take my word for it.

The consequence is worth sitting with, because it's the uncomfortable part of this lesson: **"nearest neighbour" is not a property of your dataset.** It's a property of your dataset *and your units*. Every method that reasons from neighbours — which is nearly all of them — is sitting on top of a choice nobody made deliberately.

But notice the asymmetry. Some facts about a dataset are untouched by any invertible change of coordinates: how many independent directions actually generate the variation. Distances are not among them. That asymmetry is going to be the whole fix, and we'll come back to it — hold it in mind as an open thread.

Not quite — the invariant is the *number* of independent directions, not the directions themselves. Under an invertible linear map $A$, the covariance becomes $A\Sigma A^\top$: the rank (how many directions carry variance) is preserved, but the eigenvectors themselves move with $A$. So "the data vary in 3 independent directions" survives a change of units; "the direction is $v$" does not.

Worth adding, since the passage is loose here: that invariance holds for invertible *linear* changes, which is exactly the units/rescaling case. A nonlinear change of coordinates can change the covariance rank even while preserving intrinsic dimension — the helix computation from earlier is the local version of that.

Correct, and your reason is exactly the mechanism: the algorithm is blind to which $f$ is true, so it cannot help but be fooled.

## What that establishes

The argument never touched dimension, which is the part that reorganizes everything. So:

> [!IMPORTANT]
> An assumption is **mandatory in every dimension**. Dimension does not decide *whether* you need one — it decides what one **costs**.

That is the hinge. It means "the curse of dimensionality" was never a claim that learning is impossible in high dimension. Learning is *equally* impossible in one dimension without an assumption. The curse is that the assumptions which are cheap in low dimension get expensive as dimension grows, and the exchange rate is exponential.

Here's the whole landscape in one table — every row is something you already understand now, and the last row is where we're headed:

| what you assume about $f$ | what a guarantee costs |
|---|---|
| nothing | impossible — no sample count suffices |
| exactly linear in $D$ features | $D+1$ points determine it exactly, no $\varepsilon$ at all |
| changes at rate $L$ per Euclidean unit in $\mathbb{R}^D$ | $\sim(L/\varepsilon)^{D}$ samples |
| changes at rate $L$ per unit of distance **along $\mathcal{M}$**, with $\mathcal{M}$ of dimension $k$ | $\sim(L/\varepsilon)^{k}$ samples |

Read the table downward and the trade is visible: **rigidity buys discount**. The linear model is the cheapest guarantee there is, and it's cheap precisely because it claims the most — it doesn't merely bound how fast $f$ can move, it dictates the exact form. The Lipschitz assumption on $\mathbb{R}^D$ claims much less, so it costs exponentially more. The manifold row claims something structural instead of something parametric, and that's the bargain the second half of this lesson is about.

One honest amendment on adaptivity: it doesn't create structure, but it does exploit it. Given an assumption, active sampling can beat the passive count. It just can't substitute for the assumption.

messages.text: Not generally — a metric is one *family* of assumption, not the shape of all of them. The linear row in that table isn't metric-shaped at all: it's a parametric restriction ("$f$ is exactly $w^\top x$"), which is why $D+1$ points pin it down and no $\varepsilon$ appears. What the metric does is fix the cost of the *nonparametric* assumptions: give a rate $L$ in a metric $d$, and the sample count scales as $(L/\varepsilon)^{\dim}$, where $\dim$ is the dimension of the space $d$ measures. So "assume a distance" isn't quite the assumption — it's "assume a metric **and** a rate in it"; the metric alone constrains nothing, and the pair is what sets the exponent.
sorry, I meant to say that the assumption is that distance is similar in ambient space and in the manifold, meaning that there is a bound

Half right, and the direction matters. $\lVert x-x'\rVert \le d_{\mathcal M}(x,x')$ is automatic — a straight line is never longer than a curve — so that side is free. What has to be *assumed* is the reverse, $d_{\mathcal M}(x,x')\le C\lVert x-x'\rVert$, and only locally: bounded curvature (a reach condition) gives it inside a ball, while the two-sheet example shows it fails globally. With it you get $|f(p)-f(q)|\le L\,d_{\mathcal M}\le LC\lVert p-q\rVert$, i.e. an ambient rate $LC$ — that's the bridge.

One correction to the framing, though: that comparability bound is not what produces the $(L/\varepsilon)^k$ discount. The discount comes from covering $\mathcal{M}$ itself, which needs $\varepsilon^{-k}$ balls whether or not any ambient ruler is available. The comparability bound is what lets a *neighbourhood-based* method on ambient coordinates tap into that, at the price of the constant $C$.

anchor.blockText:
Two elements of that figure to carry into the count: the blue and red charts **overlap**, so no point falls between them — the circle is covered by finitely many charts, and $2$ suffice no matter how small $\delta$ gets. And the dashed tangent at $P$ is the local $k$-plane: one per point, rotating as $P$ moves. Panel B is the failure case — a disk around the origin that no arc can cover.

## Counting on a manifold

Now the count, and it's the same arithmetic you already own, applied in the right coordinates.

Inside one chart, the manifold *is* a product of $k$ coordinates. So cover it with $(1/\delta)^k$ cells — the identical computation as the cube, with $k$ factors instead of $D$.

Then ask: how many charts? That's set by how fast the tangent plane rotates, which is a property of $\mathcal{M}$ and not of $\delta$. Fix the charts once and the same finite set works at every tolerance. So

$$N\;\approx\;(\text{number of charts})\times\left(\frac{1}{\delta}\right)^{k},$$

and the number of charts doesn't move as $\delta\to0$. Curvature, size, and shape all enter there — in the front factor — and none of them touch the exponent.

**That's what "constant" meant**, and it's what your question was asking. The circle: $2$ charts at $\delta=0.1$ giving $\sim20$ cells, $2$ charts at $\delta=0.001^\,$ giving $\sim2000$ cells. The $2$ is the constant. It is a real quantity, it depends on $\mathcal{M}$, and it is *not* irrelevant — it just doesn't grow as you demand more precision. The exponent is what governs whether the requirement is survivable, and the exponent is $k$.

One honest condition: with unbounded curvature the number of charts blows up, so no finite constant exists. That's why the theory assumes bounded curvature — a **reach** condition. It is a real assumption, not housekeeping.

And it answers your earlier question about whether "is a manifold" can be shown: whether a given dataset lies on one is empirical, judged by estimation tools with real limitations. That's a node near the end, and the answer is more interesting than "yes".

messages.text:
A **chart** is a coordinate system laid on one patch of $\mathcal{M}$: a map $\phi: U \to \mathbb{R}^k$ from a neighborhood $U\subset\mathcal{M}$ onto an open set in $\mathbb{R}^k$, smooth with smooth inverse. It hands each point $p\in U$ a $k$-tuple of numbers — coordinates — and you can go back and forth without loss.

Example, the circle: on the upper arc, $\phi(x,y)=x$ is a chart (the arc projects one-to-one onto $(-1,1)$). It fails on the full circle, since $x$ doesn't distinguish top from bottom — hence the second chart.

Two things it isn't: it's local (a chart covers a patch, never the whole circle), and it isn't the tangent plane — the chart is a curved patch's *labelling*, the tangent plane is its flat linearization at one point.
